newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungarian sell-offs unhurt by scandal - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Hungarian sell-offs unhurt by scandal - analysts.

text.p: Hungary's privatisation scandal has important political repercussions but should have little impact on the privatisation process itself, most analysts and investors said on Monday.
Csaba Varga of Citibank said the impact of the scandal, which forced the sacking of Industry and Trade Minister Tamas Suchman, will be much larger on domestic politics than on privatisation.
"It wasn't bad practice that caused the scandal. If there was trouble, it was with the high level of corruption," Varga said.

"The direction of privatisation will remain unchanged, I do not expect substantial change," Peter Muszely of Concorde Securities told Reuters. "The privatisation deals in process will certainly continue."

Suchman had been the only high official of privatisation agency APV Rt spared on Friday when the government sacked all members of APV's executive and supervisory boards in a scandal over payments amounting to more than 800 million forints ($5.2 million) to consultant Marta Tocsik.

But Prime Minister Gyula Horn, after coming under intense pressure from his coalition government partners the Free Democrats as well as elements inside his own Socialist Party, said on Sunday that Suchman would be removed from his post as of October 15.
"It could do much harm to the government ahead of the 1998 elections but I expect that corruption will be reduced as a result of this case," Varga said.

Varga added that the replacement of minister in charge of privatisation and the APV board, which he expected to be complete within two weeks, could cause some delay in implementing future APV decisions.
"The new minister is likely to introduce much stricter control on privatisation, which may make the process slower," he said.

But another lawyer involved in privatisations, who asked not to be named, said "it would be a miracle" to get another board so quickly and added the privatisation process could become "very difficult".

Pierre Abou of Electricite de France, which bought large stakes in two regional electricity distributors in December last year, said the scandal had little bearing on EdF's investment plans in Hungary.

The EdF purchase was part of a $2 billion sell-off of utilities in December 1995 which put Hungary at the forefront of post-communist large scale privatisation and boosted the reputation of the APV and Suchman.
Tamas Simonyi of Girocredit noted prices on the Budapest Stock Exchange held up on Monday.
The BUX index of the Budapest Stock Exchange actually hit a record high on Monday of 3,634.80 points, up 26.79 points, bourse figures showed.
